'''Herman Rubin''' (1926–2018) was an American [[statistician]] and [[mathematician]], professor at [[Purdue University]]. He died in 2018 at the age of 91.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Herman Rubin Obituary (1926 - 2018) - West Lafayette, IN - Journal & Courier |url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/jconline/name/herman-rubin-obituary?id=23579484 |access-date=2025-09-20 |website=Legacy.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |first=Anirban|last=DasGupta|date=2018-05-15 |title=Obituary: Herman Rubin, 1926–2018|publisher=Institute of Mathematical Statistics|url=https://imstat.org/2018/05/15/obituary-herman-rubin-1926-2018/ |access-date=2025-09-20 |language=en}}</ref>

==Education and career==
Born in 1926 in [[Chicago, Illinois]], Rubin received a high school diploma in at the age of 16 in 1943, and earned his undergraduate and graduate degrees from the [[University of Chicago]], completing his doctorate in mathematics at the age of 21 in 1948; his official advisor was [[Paul Halmos]]. He served in the U.S. Army during the Second World War.<ref>{{cite journal | author-link=Mary Ellen Bock | url=https://projecteuclid.org/ebooks/institute-of-mathematical-statistics-lecture-notes-monograph-series/A-Festschrift-for-Herman-Rubin/chapter/Conversations-with-Herman-Rubin/10.1214/lnms/1196285408.pdf | title=Conversations with Herman Rubin | last=Bock | first=Mary Ellen | journal=Institute of Mathematical Statistics | series=A Festschrift for Herman Rubin | date=2004 | pages=408–417 | doi=10.1214/lnms/1196285408 | isbn=0-940600-61-7 | quote=Herman Rubin was born October 27, 1926 in Chicago, Illinois. He obtained his Ph.D. in Mathematics from the University of Chicago in 1948 at the age of 21. ~. He is well known for his broad ranging mathematical research interests and for fundamental contributions in Bayesian decision theory, in set theory, in estimations for simultaneous equations, in probability and in asymptotic statistics.}}</ref>  Prior to joining Purdue University in 1967, Rubin held faculty positions at several other prestigious institutions (Stanford University,<ref>{{Cite web |title=History of the Department {{!}} Department of Statistics |url=https://statistics.stanford.edu/about/history |access-date=2025-09-20 |website=statistics.stanford.edu}}</ref> the University of Oregon, and Michigan State University).

==Contributions to statistics==
{{Unreferenced section|date=September 2025}}
Rubin was considered a [[polymath]] with a unique ability to solve complex problems. He was a prolific researcher, publishing over 130 papers that have become standard texts in various fields. His key contributions include:
* [[Multivariate Analysis]]: He co-authored seminal papers with [[T.W. Anderson]] on the distribution theory of [[maximum likelihood estimator]]s in [[factor analysis]] and [[structural equation model]]s.
* [[Monotone likelihood ratio]]: He is credited with the widely used and fundamental concept of monotone likelihood ratio families.
* [[Bayesian Inference]]: Rubin was a lifelong [[Bayesian]] statistician who took the theory and axioms of [[Leonard Jimmie Savage]] literally, and he contributed significantly to the theory of [[Bayes risk]]s.
* [[Econometrics]]: He worked on problems related to the [[simultaneous equations model]] in economics, including the development of the [[Simultaneous equations model#Limited information maximum likelihood (LIML)|Limited information maximum likelihood]] (LIML) estimator.
* [[Set Theory]] and Probability: His work also included contributions to set theory, the [[Large deviations theory#Moderate deviations for sums of independent random variables|theory of moderate deviations]], and the characterization of probability distributions.
* [[Hypothesis testing]]: in collaboration with [[Samuel Karlin]], the [[Uniformly most powerful test#The Karlin%E2%80%93Rubin theorem|Karlin-Rubin theorem]] provides a method for finding uniformly most powerful tests for one-sided hypotheses, a significant contribution to the theory of hypothesis testing.

He was an inaugural Fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]] and a Fellow of the [[Institute of Mathematical Statistics]].

==Family==
{{Unreferenced section|date=September 2025}}
He was married to [[Jean E. Rubin]] (1926–2002), a professor of mathematics at Purdue University whose primary research focus was on the [[axiom of choice]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jean E. Rubin Obituary |url=https://resources.illc.uva.nl/LogicList/newsitem.php?id=351 |access-date=2025-09-20 |website=resources.illc.uva.nl}}</ref> His son [[Arthur Rubin]] (born 1956) is a mathematician and aerospace engineer.

==Legacy==
A memorial lecture series, the Herman Rubin Memorial Lecture, was established at Purdue University in his honor.<ref>{{Cite web |title=In Memory of Herman Rubin - Department of Statistics - Purdue University |url=https://www.stat.purdue.edu/giving/rubin.html |access-date=2025-09-20 |website=www.stat.purdue.edu}}</ref>
